paras: The sale of John Hanson was the public auction of a Black man into a year's servitude at the courthouse door in Louisville, Kentucky, on June 14, 1882, as punishment for vagrancy. A city scavenger bought him for two dollars. Papers across the country reported it as a return of slavery, the first such sale in the city since before the Civil War.

According to a Louisville special dispatch, Hanson was convicted of vagrancy before a Justice's court, which sent the case to the Circuit Court for sentence. A separate Louisville dispatch said Judge Jackson had rendered the judgment on the 5th "upon indisputable proof that Hanson was a vagrant." The sentence rested on a law dating to 1795, whose vagrancy section, as the dispatch quoted it, provided that persons indicted for vagrancy "shall be tried by a jury" and, if guilty, sold into servitude for up to a year. A notice posted on the courthouse door advertised him as "an able-bodied man of color, about 40 years of age," sound except for rheumatism in his legs.

Despite a threatening storm, a crowd the second dispatch put at about 500, many of them Black, gathered at the courthouse door. At noon the Sheriff arrived with Hanson, who was placed on a chair while several men felt his arms and legs and asked how much work he could do. Bidding opened at fifty cents and rose by nickels to $1.15, when a city scavenger offered two dollars and took him unopposed. Hanson said nothing to the crowd's hoots and followed the buyer away.

The special dispatch stated that under state law the buyer held the power of a slaveholder and could whip Hanson, and that the sentencing judge meant to sentence every vagrant before him the same way. Black onlookers were described as "much excited" and making "bitter remarks," though the Springfield Republican noted there was no disturbance. No report of Hanson's later fate, of the buyer's name, or of any legal challenge appears in the coverage.

Coverage came entirely from white papers, spreading from June 17 to July 11 through a Louisville special dispatch credited variously to the New York Times and to the Tribune. Out-of-state papers ran it under headings such as "Slavery Days Recalled," "Human Slavery," and "A Return to Old Times." The dispatch closed by calling the law in "direct conflict" with the federal Constitution and proof of the "non-progressive spirit" of Kentucky's "Bourbon" lawmakers, while it presented Black onlookers' remarks in dialect as "very amusing."

The Rugbeian of Tennessee closed its paragraph with "Shade of Lincoln!" Kentucky papers, by contrast, gave the sale a single line among state news items without comment. The Springfield Republican described the statute as one under which "negroes convicted of vagrancy" could be sold, a racial limit not found in the text the dispatch quoted.

The Rugbeian dated the sentence to "last Wednesday," the same day the second dispatch gave for the sale, which it placed nine days after Judge Jackson's judgment. The special dispatch reported a Justice's conviction and a Circuit Court sentence but no jury trial, although the statute it quoted called for one.

reader.title: Sale of John Hanson
bases: A Black man convicted of vagrancy was sold by court order at public auction into a year's servitude to a city scavenger (A2, A6, A8).

Two separate Louisville dispatches (the special dispatch in A2 and the 'dispatch of the 14th' in A6) and independent briefs (A1, A4, A8) agree on the sale of John Hanson at the courthouse door for one year.

accounts.gist: Detailed scene of the auction, the bidding, the onlookers' remarks in dialect, and the purchaser's power over Hanson, closing with an attack on Kentucky's 'Bourbon' lawmakers.

accounts.label: Louisville dispatch of the 14th
accounts.gist: Briefer report giving the noon sale, a crowd of about 500, and Judge Jackson's judgment of the 5th.

framing.detail: The special dispatch called the law in 'direct conflict' with the U.S. Constitution and the case proof of Kentucky's 'stagnation', while mocking Black onlookers' remarks as 'very amusing'.
The Rugbeian ended its paragraph 'Shade of Lincoln!'
Kentucky papers printed one-line briefs without comment.
The Grant County Herald headed its item 'A Return to Old Times' and called it 'the sale of a live negro'.
